theme: Esau’s line; Joseph sold into Egypt, the Christ-type
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 36:1-37:36. The first chapter is Esau’s genealogy. The second begins the Joseph narrative, the dreams, the brothers’ hatred, the selling into slavery. Read the genealogy briefly and focus your attention on chapter 37.
settingTheScene: Before turning to Joseph’s story, Genesis pauses to record Esau’s descendants, the Edomites. This is the standard biblical pattern: the line of promise narrows by first noting what happens to the other line. Esau gets a chapter. Then attention returns to Jacob’s family and to Joseph. The chapter that follows introduces one of the longest sustained narratives in the Bible, the Joseph story, which will run for thirteen chapters to the end of Genesis. Joseph is seventeen years old, his father’s favorite, gifted with prophetic dreams, and hated by his brothers. Today’s reading ends with him in chains, on his way to Egypt.
observation: Genesis 36 is the Edomite genealogy. Esau becomes a nation in his own right.
The chapter is included as a record but signals that Esau is now off the main path of God’s redemptive purposes.
Genesis 37 opens: “Jacob lived in the land of his father’s sojournings.” The journey home is complete.
Joseph is seventeen, working with his brothers, and bringing bad reports of them to his father.
Jacob loves Joseph more than the others and makes him a special robe, a “coat of many colors” or a long-sleeved garment.
Joseph has two dreams. In the first, his brothers’ sheaves bow to his. In the second, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him.
Even Jacob rebukes Joseph for the second dream, but “kept the saying in mind” (verse 11).
The brothers see Joseph approaching at Dothan and plot to kill him. Reuben tries to save him; Judah suggests selling him instead.
Joseph is sold to Ishmaelite traders for twenty shekels of silver. He is taken to Egypt.
The brothers dip his coat in goat’s blood and deceive Jacob, who “tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins.”
interpretation:
Genesis 37 begins one of the most extended narratives in the Bible. The Joseph story will run thirteen chapters and dominate the rest of Genesis. It is a story of providence, suffering, betrayal, and reversal. And it begins with one of the most dysfunctional family scenes in the Old Testament.

Joseph is seventeen. He is Rachel’s son, Jacob’s favorite wife’s firstborn, and so Jacob favors him. Jacob makes him a special robe, marking him out as the heir apparent. This favoritism is the same fault Jacob’s own parents had, and the consequences are predictable. The brothers hate Joseph. They cannot speak peaceably to him.

Joseph does not help. He tells his brothers about his dreams, dreams in which they bow down to him. He brings their father bad reports about them. He is, by any honest reading, an entitled and immature young man. The text does not glorify Joseph in his teenage years. He is being prepared by God for greatness, but he is not yet great.

The plot to kill Joseph is chilling. The brothers see him approaching at Dothan, sent by his father to check on them, and they say, “Here comes this dreamer.” They decide to kill him and throw him into a pit. Reuben, the oldest, tries to save Joseph by suggesting they not shed blood but throw him into a pit alive (intending to rescue him later). Then Judah, recognizing they could profit from selling Joseph, suggests they sell him to Ishmaelite traders. Joseph is sold for twenty shekels of silver.

This is the Old Testament’s first sale of a person for money. The price, twenty shekels, is the value of a young male slave in the ancient Near East. The deal is done quickly, and Joseph is on his way to Egypt before the brothers have even finished celebrating.

They then deceive Jacob with Joseph’s bloodied robe. The deceiver is deceived again. The same Jacob who fooled Isaac with goat skins and savory food is now fooled by his sons with goat’s blood and Joseph’s coat. The Hebrew is striking: “Identify, please”, the same words Jacob’s brothers say to him are the words Tamar will later say to Judah in chapter 38. The patterns of deception keep circling back.

Jacob’s grief is total. He tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and refuses to be comforted. “I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning.” The favorite son is gone. The light of Jacob’s life has been extinguished. He has no idea that Joseph is alive, much less that Joseph will one day save the whole family.

But notice the last sentence of the chapter. “Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.” Joseph is in Egypt. The story is not over. What looks from the ground like total loss is, from heaven’s perspective, the careful providential placement of a Hebrew son in the household of an Egyptian official. The God who promised Abraham four hundred years in Egypt is moving the pieces.
connection: Joseph’s descent into Egypt is the beginning of the fulfillment of God’s prophecy to Abram in Genesis 15:13, “your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there.” The four hundred years of Egyptian sojourning that culminates in the Exodus begins right here, with one teenage boy in chains on his way south.
application: The worst day of Joseph’s life, being sold into slavery by his own brothers, was the start of God’s plan to save his family. This is sobering and hopeful. The events that seem most catastrophic in your life may be the very means by which God is positioning you for what he intends to do. You may not see it. Joseph certainly did not see it as the chains were clinking. But God’s hand is in things you cannot trace.
prayerPrompts: Tell God about a hardship, betrayal, or loss that you cannot yet make sense of.
Ask him to help you trust that he is at work even when you cannot see it.
Ask for eyes to see later what he was doing.
